blocks.eyebrow: Chapter 2 - Making a ledger out of it
blocks.heading: There are no balances
text: Caleb opens his wallet to pay Nora. It says 0.0812 BTC.
That number is not stored anywhere. His wallet worked it out, and the network has never heard of it.

blocks.heading: What is actually stored
text: Every node keeps a set of **unspent outputs**. Each one is an amount and a condition for unlocking it. That set is the entire state of the system.
A wallet scans it for outputs it can unlock and adds them up. The total is a summary it made for you.

blocks.heading: So he cannot send 0.05
text: He has one output, worth 0.0812, and outputs are consumed whole. There is no way to spend part of one.
To pay Nora he destroys his coin entirely and creates two new ones.

blocks.alt: One input of 0.0812 BTC splitting into an output of 0.05 to Nora and 0.0309 change to Caleb, with a fee of 0.0003 shown as the remainder
blocks.caption: 0.05 to Nora, 0.0309 back to himself. The 0.0003 that is missing is the fee.

blocks.title: The fee is not a field
text: Nothing in the transaction states it. There is no `fee:` anywhere in the format.
The fee is whatever the inputs exceed the outputs by, and the miner takes it. Which means forgetting the change output is not an error - it is a very large tip.

blocks.question: If nobody writes down the fee, what stops Caleb from creating an output of 0.0812 to Nora _and_ one of 0.03 to himself?
answer: Every node checks that the inputs cover the outputs before relaying anything. It is the one arithmetic rule the whole system rests on: money out cannot exceed money in.
Fail it and the transaction is not rejected by a referee - it is simply never forwarded by anyone.

blocks.heading: The shape of a transaction
text: Inputs are pointers - which earlier output, and which position in it. Outputs are amounts with conditions. Nothing else is needed.

blocks.label: the payment, stripped to its structure
blocks.code:
in:   (txid 9c1f...4a2b, index 0)     0.0812
out:  0.05     -> lock to Nora's address
out:  0.0309   -> lock to Caleb's change address

blocks.heading: The day the rule held and the code did not
text: Block 74,638 carried a transaction with two outputs of about **92.2 billion BTC** each.
Added together in a signed 64-bit integer, they overflowed to a negative number. The check `inputs >= outputs` compared against that, and passed.
Patched within hours. The corrected clients rejected the block, and the honest chain overtook the bad one inside a day.
The rule was right; the arithmetic implementing it was not. That distinction is worth carrying into every security argument in this course.

blocks.heading: The one transaction with no inputs
text: Each block begins with a coinbase transaction, which spends nothing and creates the block subsidy plus every fee in that block.
It is the only place bitcoin comes from. Every other satoshi traces back through a chain of spends to one of these.

blocks.heading: What the change output gives away

text: Caleb's 0.0309 goes to a fresh address he controls, which looks like a second payment to a stranger. It is not: it sits in the same transaction as the real one.
That co-occurrence is exactly what chain-analysis firms exploit. Chapter 5 comes back to it.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: Your balance is a number your wallet computed; what exists on the network is a pile of individually locked coins.
Caleb's wallet has built the transaction. Now it has to sign it - and what exactly the signature reaches around turns out to be a design decision.
